analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators claw back pay from executives of failed banks and bar them from banking.
analysis.headline: Six senators sponsored the bill across party lines and the Banking Committee held one hearing in May 2023, but it never got a committee vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a bank fails, the FDIC takes it over and pays depositors from its insurance fund, and the executives who ran it into the ground typically keep the pay and bonuses they already collected. This bill would let the FDIC recover up to two years of that pay from senior executives and directors who were substantially responsible for the failure, with no time limit in fraud cases. It would also bar those individuals from working in any financial company for at least two years, stop liability insurers from covering the clawback on their behalf, and make it easier to ban executives at the largest failing financial firms.
analysis.who_benefits: The FDIC's insurance fund and the taxpayers who backstop it in large failures, along with depositors of failed banks, gain because executives who wreck a bank share the cost instead of walking away with salary, bonuses, and golden parachutes intact.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and depositors in failed banks

how_it_helps.text: The FDIC could recover compensation paid during the two years before it took a failed bank into receivership from any senior executive or director substantially responsible for the failure, with no time limit where fraud was involved.
Liability insurance policies could no longer cover an executive's clawback liability, so the money comes out of the executive's own pocket rather than an insurer's.

The FDIC could bar such executives from participating in the affairs of any financial company for at least two years, and the bill removes the requirement that a violation involve 'personal dishonesty' before executives of the largest failing firms can be banned by the Fed and FDIC.

analysis.who_pays: Senior executives and directors of failed banks, who would surrender up to two years of compensation and face industry bans, plus the insurers who currently sell them coverage for these situations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Executives and directors of failed banks

drawbacks.text: Broad triggers, such as any 'unsafe or unsound practice' or breach of fiduciary duty, give the FDIC wide discretion, and the industry-ban duration has a two-year floor but no fixed ceiling, which could make it harder to recruit qualified people to serve as bank directors and executives.

The bill directs the FDIC to weigh the financial and deterrent benefits of a clawback against the cost of pursuing it, which means recovery is not automatic and could be skipped when cases are expensive to litigate.
A two-year lookback may not reach compensation from failures that built up over many years, such as those caused by long-run strategic mismanagement rather than recent conduct.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are targeted and real: executives who preside over a bank collapse would no longer keep two years of pay at the expense of the FDIC fund, and the removal of the dishonesty requirement makes bans easier at the largest firms. The costs are limited but genuine: broad, discretionary triggers could deter capable people from bank leadership, and recovery is not guaranteed because the FDIC must weigh the cost of suing. On balance a fairly narrow accountability measure rather than a sweeping overhaul.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Banking Committee held one hearing on the bill in May 2023, never voted to send it to the floor, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Jack Reed introduced the bill on April 18, 2023, together with Sen. Chuck Grassley, and it was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee.
Five senators cosponsored the bill, four Democrats and one Republican.
The committee held a hearing on May 4, 2023, but that was the last recorded action; no markup or vote ever occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Senior executives and directors of failed banks are better off, because they keep the compensation they earned in the years before a failure and face no industry ban; the insurers who write their liability coverage also keep that business.

industries.industry: Senior executives and directors of failed banks
industries.note: These officials would surrender up to two years of compensation and face at least a two-year industry ban when they are substantially responsible for a failure. Today their gain is compensation retained while the FDIC fund absorbs the bank's collapse.
The bill bars liability policies from covering clawback liability, eliminating a category of coverage these insurers sell to bank executives and directors.
Stated purpose is improving financial stability; personal accountability for failed-bank leadership deters risky management and protects the insurance fund that all banks contribute to.
